title: Toto Wolff Backs Human Instinct Over Data As Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Powers Mercedes F1's AI Race Machine - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 21, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis When ten million simulations point one way and the driver says another, Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team Principal Toto Wolff has a clear answer: trust the human. Wolff and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Commercial Business CEO Judson Althoff spoke with Yahoo Finance on November 20, outlining the scope of artificial intelligence now embedded across the Mercedes F1 operation. The partnership spans car design, factory workflows, personnel management, and race-day strategy, representing one of the most compute-intensive deployments in professional motorsport. Althoff described a layered infrastructure in which analysts based in the United Kingdom, engineers in the pit garage, and the driver in the cockpit must all align within millisecond windows during a race. The Singapore Grand Prix offered a vivid illustration, with Wolff and his team working through rapid-fire calculations about precisely when driver Kimi should make a passing move under live race conditions. More than 10 million race-day simulations run behind that kind of decision, feeding a compute fabric that Althoff said most people outside the sport would struggle to fully appreciate in terms of sheer pressure and intensity. Yet for all that processing power, the most persistent tension inside the team is not a technical one — it is the long-running friction between what sensors record and what a driver physically feels. Wolff, who positions himself as a mediator between the data-driven engineering culture and the instinct-driven world of the driver, described the conflict as predating the current wave of AI entirely. “It was always a theme, even before AI, that the engineer would say, this is what the car does and the driver say, no, no, it doesn’t do that,” Wolff said, describing a divide that better algorithms have not closed. His resolution to that conflict carries weight given Mercedes’ investment in machine intelligence: when data and human judgment diverge, the driver wins. “I’m siding with the human because the human needs to drive the car and the human needs to feel the confidence in driving it,” Wolff said, adding that driver preference overrides what the numbers might identify as the faster setup. Wolff framed the driver as the team’s single most valuable sensor, describing the person behind the wheel as “the one that sits in the car” — and the most expensive instrument Mercedes deploys. The stance raises a broader question for organizations racing to automate decision-making: at what point does accumulated data become less reliable than embodied human experience operating under extreme conditions. For Mercedes, at least at race speed, that threshold has already been defined — no simulation, however vast, outranks the judgment of the driver holding the wheel. For the December quarter, Microsoft guides revenue to $96.0–97.1B, growth of 18–19%. The growth is concentrated in the cloud. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9B, up 30%, with growth accelerating. Azure grew 48%, even though some third-party capacity deliveries slipped. Commercial remaining performance obligations, the contracted backlog, rose 73% to $677B. About 30% of that should turn into revenue within twelve months. Copilot is starting to show up in the numbers. Daily users rose nearly 50% from the prior quarter and more than fivefold from a year ago. The number of customers with more than 50,000 seats is up more than eightfold, and Volkswagen plans to roll Copilot out to over 330,000 employees. The weak spot is the PC. Windows OEM revenue fell 27% as the market digested last year's Windows 10 upgrade cycle and memory costs pushed up PC prices. Management guides Windows OEM and devices down in the mid-30s next quarter. Xbox revenue fell 2%. This is what separates Microsoft from the rest of the group. Over the past twelve months, Microsoft generated about $60B of free cash flow. Meta generated $28.7B and Alphabet $19.7B, while Amazon burned $46.9B. Microsoft spent 69% of its operating cash flow on capex, the lowest share of the four. As The Motley Fool noted this week, it is the only one of them forecasting positive free cash flow next year. Capex is still climbing fast. Cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4B in the quarter. Including $7.4B of finance leases, total capex was $45.2B. For calendar 2026, capex should come in around $170B, and the CFO expects more than $50B next quarter. Operating cash flow is keeping pace, though: it rose 29% to $58.0B. title: Tech Outages At Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) And Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) Cast Shadow Over Mullin's Global Threat Testimony - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 20, 2026 | Featured, News & Analysis, Politics A cascading wave of widespread technology failures at some of America’s largest companies has set an uneasy backdrop for high-stakes congressional oversight hearings in Washington. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is facing pointed questioning from lawmakers on Capitol Hill over the administration’s assessment of worldwide security threats. The timing of his appearance has drawn heightened scrutiny given the recent rash of major outages that disrupted services across Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), and several major airline networks. Those failures have renewed urgent questions about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure and whether the country’s technology backbone is adequately protected against both accidental and deliberate disruption. Space Force chief software officer Nicolas Chaillan weighed in on the situation, offering his perspective on the wave of tech failures and what they signal about broader systemic vulnerabilities. Chaillan’s comments underline a growing concern among defense and security professionals that widespread outages, regardless of their origin, expose dangerous fragility in systems that underpin everyday life. Airline networks were among the most visible casualties of the disruptions, with passengers facing delays and service interruptions that rippled across the broader transportation sector. For Mullin, the outages represent an unavoidable talking point as he confronts legislators eager to probe whether the federal government has a credible plan to prevent or respond to large-scale infrastructure failures. The convergence of a global threat briefing with fresh evidence of domestic technological fragility is likely to shape the tone and focus of the committee’s line of questioning considerably. Capitol Hill hearings on national security have increasingly expanded their scope to include cyber resilience and the private sector’s role in safeguarding infrastructure that millions of Americans depend on daily. The Mullin testimony arrives at a moment when policymakers are under pressure to demonstrate that oversight mechanisms can keep pace with the speed and scale of modern technological disruption. Whether the recent outages were the result of technical failures, cyberattacks, or some combination of both remains a central question that lawmakers are expected to press Mullin to answer directly. "We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don't have control of their own destiny because [of] the way we have talked about this AI revolution." Nadella explained how Microsoft's evolving acceptance of AI influenced this decision. "Let's take software engineering. We went from, 'Well, we don't buy that AI can ever do software.' To suddenly, 'Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?' To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point," Nadella told Sorkin. For some employees, "that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?" said Nadella, who added that, in his opinion, "it has to be done." Nadella believes at some point, every employee that uses a computer will manage AI agents instead of doing the work themselves. "That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs," he told Sorkin. But until then, the 60,000 Microsoft employees who were given voluntary buyouts have to make a decision on whether to accept the company's offer before the deadline in early December. Voluntary buyouts can reduce the need for — or size of — layoffs, which can be good for companies that want to avoid the stress and stigma of laying off swaths of workers. For employees, a voluntary buyout can provide several benefits. First, some employees may already be looking at their options and have considered leaving their current employer. Second, some employees who receive buyout offers might feel as if they won't have a difficult time finding a new position elsewhere. And third, employees who want to stay at the company may be less likely to be laid off in the future if enough of their colleagues take the buyout. "How much you should have in reserves, whether you have a spouse or significant other or life partner that's helping with taking care of some of those expenses, should things go longer than expected." "Taxes play a major part in it as well," he adds. "The last thing you want is for the taxes to be paid, but you're still significantly short, because this lump sum number threw you into a new tax bracket." You should also think about the state of the company before making a decision. "The person who's best qualified to answer that is the person who's been in the kitchen to see how the sausage is made," said Lee. "Is your department returning a profit? Are you seeing young people being hired into your department? You have to put your CEO hat on and really determine, you know, is my department needed?" In some cases, it might be tempting to pivot your retirement plans if you get a buyout offer. That delay makes Microsoft’s own forecast harder to hit. Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, ahead of management’s expectations. For fiscal Q2, management guided for even faster Azure growth of 49% to 50% at constant exchange rates. But some supply it expected in that quarter has moved out. So the company is counting on getting more work out of the chips it already runs to get there. The risk is not that customers walk away, but that Microsoft cannot serve them as fast as management has forecast. Microsoft Cloud, where Azure sits, brought in $63.9 billion of the company’s $92.3 billion in revenue in fiscal Q1 2027. So more than two thirds of the company’s sales come from Microsoft Cloud. Management said Microsoft Cloud’s growth accelerated to 30%. At that size, each 1% drop in Microsoft Cloud’s quarterly sales would be about $640 million. That is a drop in the sales themselves, not in their growth rate. Microsoft’s valuation is not near its own peak. The stock trades at 25.9 times its earnings over the past twelve months, against 21.5 for the S&P 500. Over the past 40 fiscal quarter ends, its multiple has run from 20.7 in June 2026 to 47.7 in December 2017. So the price appears to assume steady growth. It sits much nearer the bottom of that range than the top. Is Microsoft’s Supply Problem Only A Matter Of Timing? Based on what management has said, it mostly is. Demand remains intact, and the delayed contracts are now expected in the second half of the fiscal year. Management also expects free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, to stay positive in fiscal 2027. It expects that even as capital spending speeds up in that half. The risk to a holder is a quarter or two of Azure growth below management’s forecast. Microsoft stock has also often fallen harder than the S&P 500 in rough markets. During the 2022 inflation shock and Fed tightening, the shares fell 32% against 24% for the index. They dropped 15% against 7.8% in the July to August 2024 yen shock. The supply problem amounts to a delay in serving customers rather than a loss of them. Microsoft is expected to report fiscal Q2 2027 results in January 2027. The company has detailed plans to add vast new capacity across its global network, a move that speaks directly to the question dominating the market this week: how quickly, and how durably, AI-infrastructure spending will keep scaling. For readers who follow Bluechip Stocks, Microsoft remains a closely watched name in the group. The expansion push builds on a stretch in which Microsoft's cloud arm has grown briskly, carried by enterprises moving workloads to Azure and by a wave of demand tied to generative-AI features woven across the company's software. Management has framed the added capacity as a response to that demand rather than a speculative bet, pointing to utilization across its data-center fleet as the reason more campuses are coming online. The backdrop into which this news landed has been unsettled. The artificial-intelligence trade is being tested after a sharp advance, semiconductor names have seesawed, and Federal Reserve meeting minutes have kept rate expectations in flux against a thin economic-data calendar. Sentiment has been choppy, and the market's front-running groups have rotated as traders reassess how much of the AI story is already priced in. Microsoft operates one of the broadest franchises in technology, spanning the Windows platform, the Office productivity suite, the Azure cloud, LinkedIn, the Dynamics business applications, security offerings and a gaming arm anchored by Xbox. That spread gives the company multiple engines of growth and a deep, recurring relationship with enterprises and consumers alike. Microsoft sits in a rare spot: it owns both the applications many organizations run every day and a growing share of the infrastructure those applications increasingly depend on. That dual position lets the company capture demand at several layers of the stack, from the software a worker touches to the servers humming in a distant data center, and it is the reason the name is treated as a core position within the broad market. The headline development is the scale of the capacity being added. Microsoft has outlined plans to expand its data-center fleet substantially, with new campuses designed around the power and cooling demands of dense AI computing. The build-out is a concrete expression of how the company expects demand to unfold, and it has become a focal point for a market trying to gauge the durability of the broader spending wave. Executing a build-out of this magnitude is an operational challenge in its own right. Sourcing components, securing power, constructing campuses on schedule and bringing capacity online efficiently all bear on how smoothly demand is met, and the market watches those details closely because they shape how quickly the company can convert surging interest into live services. The hyperscale race carries real challenges. Building at scale demands enormous capital, access to power and a steady supply of specialized chips, and any bottleneck in those inputs can slow the pace of expansion. Energy availability in particular has become a gating factor, with demand for electricity around data centers climbing even as grids strain to keep up. Microsoft competes with the other hyperscale cloud providers for enterprise workloads, with a wide field of software firms across productivity and business applications, and with a growing roster of AI specialists. What distinguishes its position is the way its software estate and its cloud infrastructure reinforce each other, so that demand for one tends to pull through demand for the other. Because of its size and its central role in the cloud and AI story, Microsoft functions as a barometer for enterprise technology spending as a whole. When the company signals that it is building capacity to meet demand, the market reads it as a vote of confidence in the durability of the AI transition, and that signal ripples across suppliers, power providers and the wider technology complex. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He's not saying he's replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He's saying he's reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI. The buyout was "to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit. "Let's take software engineering. We went from, 'Well, we don't buy that AI can ever do software.' To suddenly, 'Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?' To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point," he explained. For some people, "that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?" he added, "but, I mean, it has to be done." He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product." He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. "That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs." But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn't grow up as an AI-first company. "So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?" he said. "It's going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, 'Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.'" When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, "We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don't have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution." He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. "All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity." In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere.
